title: Currency of the Thirteen Colonies
summary: Before the dollar, money depended on where you stood.
introduction: There was no single colonial currency. A pound changed value from colony to colony, foreign coins circulated everywhere, and each paper issue carried its own legal and financial terms.

map.credit: John Mitchell, Thomas Kitchin, and Jefferys and Faden, 1775 · Library of Congress, Geography and Map Division

interpretation.title: How to read colonial money
introduction: Colonial notes become easier to understand once five questions are separated: What unit names the amount? What could settle it? Who issued the paper? Why would someone accept it? How was it meant to leave circulation?
Open the numbered tabs beside the map for a short guide, then choose a colony to read the story behind that position.

concepts.title: Why the same coin had different prices
paragraphs: Everywhere in the £sd system, twenty shillings made a pound and twelve pence made a shilling. The arithmetic stayed fixed; the value of a local pound did not.

Near the Revolution, one Spanish dollar counted as roughly 6 shillings in New England, 8 in New York, 7s6d in Philadelphia and 32s6d in Charleston. The silver coin was unchanged. Each colony's accounting scale described it differently.
concepts.callout: Do not assume that a colonial pound means sterling.

concepts.title: The price was not the payment
paragraphs: A debt recorded as £2 10s did not have to be paid with British coins—or even with paper bearing that amount. Spanish silver, other foreign coins, paper notes, commodities and book credit could all settle an account.
The denomination told people how much was owed. Local practice determined what they could hand over to pay it.

facts.label: Unit of account
facts.text: The language in which a debt is measured

facts.label: Medium of payment
facts.text: The thing accepted to settle that debt

concepts.title: Foreign silver needed a local rating
paragraphs: Spanish dollars circulated widely, but a colony still had to translate them into local shillings and pence. Those ratings linked an internationally familiar silver coin to a local accounting system.

“Proclamation Money” refers to an attempted standard based on a 1704 royal proclamation. When the phrase appears on a North Carolina bill, it tells the holder which coin-rating rule governs the paper's stated value.

concepts.title: How governments put paper into circulation
paragraphs: A legislature could spend new bills on soldiers, supplies or public work, then collect them back through later taxes. Paper let the government obtain resources before the matching revenue arrived.
A public Loan Office could instead lend notes against land or other collateral. Borrowers carried the paper into the economy and returned it through repayments. Some issues combined both methods.

facts.label: Spend it
facts.text: Government expenditure followed by tax return and cancellation

facts.label: Lend it
facts.text: Public loans followed by scheduled borrower repayments

concepts.title: Why people accepted the paper
paragraphs: No single mechanism “backed” every note. A law might require acceptance for certain debts. A government might take the note for taxes. An issue might promise later payment in silver, gold or sterling bills. A printed coin or silver equivalent could simply define value rather than promise immediate exchange.
These properties must be read separately. Maryland's 1774 paper, for example, was not legal tender but carried a specific future sterling payment rate.

concepts.title: How a note was meant to disappear
paragraphs: Colonial paper was often temporary. Government-spent bills returned through taxes; Loan Office paper returned through repayments; other notes were redeemed, exchanged for a later issue or invalidated after a deadline.
Treasuries cancelled returned notes by punching, slashing or cutting them. On a surviving note, those marks may record the successful end of the obligation rather than accidental damage.

concepts.title: What Britain restricted
paragraphs: The Currency Act of 1764 did not ban every paper issue. It chiefly prevented colonies from making new bills legal tender for private debts and from extending the legal-tender life of older issues.
Parliament eased the rule for public debts in 1773. That distinction helps explain why late colonial paper could circulate while explicitly stating that it was not legal tender.

concepts.title: Read the Maryland four-dollar note
paragraphs: The face says four dollars; the issue promised payment at 4s6d sterling per dollar. Four dollars therefore equaled eighteen shillings sterling.
The dollar is the note's denomination. Sterling states its promised settlement value. Because the issue was not legal tender, that future payment structure mattered directly to its credibility.

interpretation.relatedIntroduction: The colonies were not monetary islands. Spanish silver, sterling bills and Portuguese gold crossed borders, while French North America developed its own experiments with paper and credit.

story.subtitle: Three kinds of shillings at once
paragraphs: New Hampshire began issuing paper in 1709, but decades of reissues and reforms left Old Tenor, New Tenor and Sterling notes circulating together by 1759. A user could not interpret “shillings” from the number alone; the note's monetary standard determined what those shillings were worth.
story.collectingGoal: Best collecting target: a note that names its tenor or sterling standard clearly enough to make the competing scales visible.

story.subtitle: First to issue paper, then determined to remove it
paragraphs: Massachusetts Bay issued £7,000 after a failed 1690 expedition to Canada—the first government paper currency in English North America. By 1750 the colony was trying to restore payment in specie and exclude neighboring paper. Revolution forced another reversal in 1775, when wartime need brought government notes back.
story.collectingGoal: Best collecting target: a note that captures one of those turns—first issue, specie reform or wartime return.

story.subtitle: Money with an expiration date
paragraphs: Rhode Island authorized £13,300 for the 1710 Annapolis Royal expedition. The bills were legal tender, receivable for taxes and scheduled for redemption after five years. Counterfeiting forced a final invalidation date in 1719. This is paper designed with an entrance, a return path and an end.
story.collectingGoal: Best collecting target: a note whose redemption or invalidation language makes that lifecycle visible.

story.subtitle: A note that earned interest
paragraphs: Connecticut's 1780 Treasury Notes were circulating pieces of state debt. This ten-shilling note promised payment in Spanish milled dollars by March 1, 1785 and earned 5 percent annual interest until then. Its denomination says how much the state owed; its maturity and interest clauses say how the obligation would end.

reading.title: Read the note
paragraphs: This is closer to a small government bond than to a modern banknote: it names a debt, earns interest and has a maturity date.

story.lookClosely: A slash or punched hole can indicate successful redemption, transforming an active claim into evidence that the claim had already been discharged.

story.subtitle: A Spanish dollar worth eight shillings
paragraphs: New York issued paper in local pounds, shillings and pence while Spanish silver circulated beside it. A Spanish dollar commonly counted as eight New York shillings, so its one-real fraction matched one local shilling. Revolutionary issues later adopted the dollar itself as the printed denomination.
story.collectingGoal: Best collecting target: either a £sd note with a clear specie reference or an issue from the transition to dollar denominations.

story.subtitle: A counterfeit built to pass
paragraphs: New Jersey's authorized 1763 notes paired a local denomination with a stated weight of silver and used mica-flaked paper as a security feature. This twelve-shilling specimen is a contemporary counterfeit. Its importance lies in the imitation: someone reproduced enough of the official note's appearance and monetary language to try to make false paper circulate.

facts.label: Form
facts.text: Contemporary counterfeit of a Bill of Credit

reading.title: Read the note
paragraphs: The silver weight defines the denomination; it does not necessarily promise immediate exchange at the treasury. The counterfeit asks a different question: which visual and verbal signals made a purported bill recognizable enough to accept?

story.lookClosely: The 1763 issue introduced mica-flaked paper to New Jersey currency. This counterfeit invites comparison between the security material and the imitation of official design.

story.subtitle: Paper for an army
paragraphs: Pennsylvania authorized £200,000 of this 1777 issue for army support. The Commonwealth could pay for supplies immediately and deal with the paper's return later. Subsequent laws exchanged older notes into this issue, then replaced depreciated paper at seventy-five old to one new. The object records both wartime finance and the difficult exit from it.

reading.title: Read the note
paragraphs: The note entered circulation through wartime spending. Exchange and invalidation laws later supplied its route out.

story.lookClosely: Pound denominations carried a farming scene on the reverse. John Dunlap—printer of the first broadside Declaration of Independence—printed the issue on watermarked paper.

story.subtitle: Money lent on mortgages
paragraphs: Delaware's 1723 Loan Office issued £5,000 by lending notes on real-estate mortgages at 5 percent. Borrowers put the paper into circulation and returned it through scheduled repayments. The system created currency through public lending rather than government spending.
story.collectingGoal: Best collecting target: an early Loan Office note whose text reveals the lending structure.

story.subtitle: A dollar promised in sterling
paragraphs: Maryland's 1774 paper was denominated in dollars but promised future settlement at 4s6d sterling per dollar. This four-dollar note therefore represented eighteen shillings sterling. It was not legal tender; acceptance rested instead on a defined payment rate, a funded redemption structure and confidence in the province's Loan Office.

facts.label: Printers
facts.text: Anne Catherine Green and Frederick Green

reading.title: Read the note
paragraphs: Four dollars × 4s6d sterling = 18 shillings sterling. Dollars name the paper; sterling states its promised settlement value.

story.lookClosely: The thin paper contains mica flakes and nature-print security designs. The note came from the Annapolis shop of Anne Catherine Green and her son Frederick.

story.subtitle: War broke Virginia's resistance to paper
paragraphs: Virginia resisted government paper until military expense forced a change in 1755. Its first £20,000 issue funded the French and Indian War, carried 5 percent interest and promised quick redemption. Once the barrier fell, later wars produced more paper and eventually dollar-denominated state notes.
story.collectingGoal: Best collecting target: a 1755 Treasury Note that makes Virginia's late, wartime entry into paper money tangible.

story.subtitle: Forty shillings in Proclamation Money
paragraphs: North Carolina's 1754 issue was legal tender at Proclamation Money rates. Forty shillings equals £2 in the colony's own accounting unit—not £2 sterling. “Proclamation Money” identifies the coin-rating standard used to interpret that local value. The note makes a basic rule of the exhibit visible: the arithmetic of pounds stayed constant while the monetary value of a pound changed by place.

reading.title: Read the note
paragraphs: 40 shillings = £2 North Carolina money. The phrase Proclamation Money connects that local amount to a specie standard.

story.lookClosely: The forty-shilling note carries Christ Church at Newbern. Other denominations use a butterfly, boar, swan, bear, squirrel, crown, Bible and other motifs.

story.subtitle: The most inflated colonial pound
paragraphs: South Carolina issued paper as early as 1703, but its most vivid lesson is the local pound. Near the Revolution, the same Spanish dollar worth about 6 shillings in New England counted as roughly 32s6d in Charleston. The coin was unchanged; South Carolina's accounting scale was radically different.
story.collectingGoal: Best collecting target: a £sd note that can be read beside the colony-by-colony Spanish-dollar comparison.

story.subtitle: A London claim before local paper
paragraphs: Georgia first used Sola Bills—Trustee bills of exchange that circulated locally before returning to England for payment. Provincial paper followed in 1755 through a General Loan system, with part of the issue also supporting public works. Georgia's sequence runs from a London claim to local lending and then Revolutionary state currency.
story.collectingGoal: Best collecting target: a Sola Bill, because it gives Georgia a monetary structure unlike any other colony in the exhibit.

artifacts.title: 1754 40s North Carolina Forty Shillings
artifacts.description: Forty shillings means £2 in North Carolina's local accounting system—not £2 sterling. The phrase Proclamation Money relates that local denomination to a standard expressed against specie, making the difference between a unit of account and its value standard visible on one note.
artifacts.subtitle: A local pound defined by Proclamation Money
researchNotes: The March 9, 1754 issue authorized £40,000 in legal-tender bills of credit at Proclamation Money rates.
The forty-shilling denomination shows Christ Church at Newbern and was printed from an engraved copper plate.

artifacts.title: 1763 12s New Jersey Colonial Note - Contemporary Counterfeit
artifacts.description: New Jersey's authorized issue translated local paper denominations into stated silver-weight equivalents. This specimen is a contemporary counterfeit: evidence that recognition, security materials and public trust were as much a part of the monetary system as the legislature's promises.

images.alt: 1763 12s New Jersey Colonial Note - Contemporary Counterfeit, photograph 1
1763 12s New Jersey Colonial Note - Contemporary Counterfeit, photograph 2

artifacts.subtitle: A silver-referenced currency, convincingly imitated
researchNotes: Recorded as Fr. NJ-156CT and identified in the collection as a contemporary counterfeit of the twelve-shilling denomination.
The December 31, 1763 authorized issue was legal tender through 1781, became invalid after 1782 and introduced mica-flaked paper to New Jersey currency.

artifacts.title: 1774 $4 Maryland Colonial Currency
artifacts.description: This note was not legal tender. Maryland instead promised future payment at 4s6d sterling per dollar, so its $4 denomination equaled 18 shillings sterling. The dollar names the paper; sterling states its settlement value.
artifacts.subtitle: Four dollars measured by a future sterling promise
researchNotes: The collection record identifies the note as Fr. MD-68, serial number 14042.
Anne Catherine Green and Frederick Green printed the issue on thin paper containing mica flakes and nature-print security designs.

artifacts.title: 1777 £4 Pennsylvania Colonial Currency
artifacts.description: Pennsylvania authorized £200,000 of this issue for army support. The Commonwealth used paper to command resources before equivalent revenue arrived; later exchange and invalidation laws completed the note's path from wartime issue to retirement.
artifacts.subtitle: Paper issued to finance an army
researchNotes: The collection record identifies the note as PA-224a, serial number 10507, with Eric P. Newman Collection provenance.
John Dunlap printed the issue. Pound denominations carried a farming scene on the reverse and the paper was watermarked PENSYL / VANIA.

artifacts.title: 1780 10 s Connecticut Colonial Note
artifacts.description: This ten-shilling Treasury Note promised payment in Spanish milled dollars by March 1, 1785 and carried 5 percent annual interest. Its denomination, maturity and interest clauses make it closer to a government security than to an indefinitely circulating modern banknote.
artifacts.subtitle: Circulating paper and an interest-bearing state debt
researchNotes: The collection record identifies the note as Fr. CT-238, serial number 3063.
Redeemed examples were commonly cancelled by slashing or punching holes through them.

artifacts.title: Banque Royale January 1, 1720. 10 Livres
artifacts.description: The Banque Royale promised to pay the bearer on sight in silver specie. Its bank liability differs from a colonial legislature's bill of credit and places British-American experiments within a wider Atlantic monetary world.
artifacts.subtitle: A bank's on-sight promise to the bearer
researchNotes: The collection record identifies the note as P-A16b and records a PMG grade of Very Fine 30.
The Banque Royale was tied to the Compagnie des Indes and French Louisiana finance, but the exhibit does not claim these notes themselves circulated in America.
